cards.front: In a person, what condition must hold for body temperature to stay steady?
cards.back: Heat lost must equal heat made, so heat storage is zero. Any surplus that cannot leave is stored and temperature rises.
cards.quote: Body temperature holds steady only while heat lost equals heat made, so that heat storage is zero.

cards.front: What sets E_max, the most heat that evaporation of sweat can remove, and what does not set it?
cards.back: The water-vapour pressure gap between wet skin and the air, plus air movement (raises it) and clothing (lowers it). Sweat rate does not set it.
cards.why: Sweat rate sets how much water is offered; the gap sets how much can leave as vapour.
cards.quote: Evaporation has a ceiling, E_max, set by the gap in water-vapour pressure between wet skin and the air

cards.front: Which human skin layer has no blood vessels, which holds the vessels, nerves and sweat glands, and which is mostly insulating fat?
cards.back: Epidermis: no blood vessels (fed by diffusion from below). Dermis: vessels, nerves and sweat glands. Hypodermis: mostly insulating fat.
cards.quote: The dermis beneath it holds the vessels, nerves and sweat glands.

cards.front: Two cyclists ride at the same workload in equally hot air, one dry, one humid. Both drip sweat. Whose core temperature keeps rising, and would their sweat rates tell you?
cards.back: The cyclist in humid air. Humid air takes up less vapour from the skin, so less heat leaves by evaporation. Sweat rate would not tell you: dripping only shows some sweat is not evaporating.
cards.quote: Sweat rate would not tell you: dripping shows only that some sweat is not evaporating.

cards.front: In the whole-body heat budget, heat production equals the metabolic rate minus {{c1::external work}}.
cards.back: External work is energy that leaves as work, such as pushing the pedals.
cards.quote: Coming in is heat production: the metabolic rate minus any energy that leaves as external work, such as pushing the pedals.
cards.section: The heat budget

cards.front: Made-up example: a cyclist has a metabolic rate of 900 W and does 150 W of external work. In cool shade, dry exchange is a loss of 30 W. Evaporation removes 650 W. What is heat storage S?
cards.back: Heat production = 900 − 150 = 750 W. Dry exchange is a loss here, so S = 750 − 30 − 650 = 70 W stored; body temperature rises.
cards.why: Dry exchange runs either way: a loss when surroundings are cooler than the skin, a gain when warmer.
cards.quote: Dry exchange, by radiation, convection and conduction, runs either way: a loss when the surroundings are cooler than the skin, a gain when they are warmer.
cards.section: The heat budget

cards.front: Why does skin blood flow act as a variable insulator?
cards.back: Blood carries core heat to the skin. Low flow forces heat to creep through tissue (a thick coat); full flow carries it straight to the surface (a thin coat).
cards.quote: Blood carries heat from the core to the skin, so the skin circulation works as an insulator whose thickness the body can change.
cards.section: Lever 1: skin blood flow, a variable insulator

cards.front: In a model of an average man with a 2 °C core-to-skin difference, about how much heat passes per m² of skin with vessels constricted versus fully open?
cards.back: About 16 W per m² constricted and 65 W per m² open: roughly four times as much.
cards.quote: with a 2 °C difference, about 16 W per m² of skin with vessels constricted and 65 W per m² with them open.
cards.section: Lever 1: skin blood flow, a variable insulator

cards.front: What nerves and transmitter constrict human skin arterioles in the cold?
cards.back: Sympathetic nerves releasing noradrenaline onto skin arterioles.
cards.quote: Vasoconstriction in the cold: sympathetic nerves release noradrenaline onto skin arterioles.
cards.section: Lever 1: skin blood flow, a variable insulator

cards.front: What is unusual about the nerves that actively dilate hairy skin vessels in heat, and how much of the dilation do they supply?
cards.back: They are sympathetic in anatomy but cholinergic (release acetylcholine, not noradrenaline). They supply 80 to 90 percent of vasodilation in hairy skin in whole-body heating.
cards.why: The mediator is an open question: acetylcholine, nitric oxide and cotransmitters each contribute.
cards.quote: sympathetic cholinergic nerves (sympathetic in anatomy, but releasing acetylcholine, not noradrenaline) actively dilate skin vessels.
cards.section: Lever 1: skin blood flow, a variable insulator

cards.front: How do vessels in the glabrous skin of palms and soles dilate with warming?
cards.back: Mainly by withdrawal of constrictor tone, much of it in arteriovenous anastomoses. Glabrous skin has no active vasodilator system.
cards.quote: The hairless (glabrous) skin of palms and soles has no active vasodilator system
cards.section: Lever 1: skin blood flow, a variable insulator

cards.front: Define the human thermoneutral zone. What is its lower limit for resting nude people in air?
cards.back: The range of air temperatures where skin blood flow alone is enough, with no regulatory change in heat production or evaporation. Lower limit about 28.5 °C.
cards.quote: The thermoneutral zone is the range of air temperatures where this lever alone is enough, with no regulatory change in heat production or evaporation.
cards.section: Lever 1: skin blood flow, a variable insulator

cards.front: A resting, nude volunteer's chamber air warms by a degree but stays inside the thermoneutral zone. Which of skin blood flow, heat production and sweating change?
cards.back: Only skin blood flow, which rises; insulation falls and more heat reaches the skin. Heat production stays at resting, and regulatory sweating begins only above the zone.
cards.why: Inside the thermoneutral zone, skin blood flow is the only lever used.
cards.quote: Below it, heat production must rise; above it, regulatory sweating begins.
cards.section: Lever 1: skin blood flow, a variable insulator

cards.front: In humans, which transmitter and receptor drive thermal sweating by eccrine glands?
cards.back: Acetylcholine from sympathetic postganglionic fibres, acting on muscarinic receptors of the gland. Apocrine glands are not thermoregulatory.
cards.quote: As in active vasodilation, the nerves are sympathetic but the transmitter is acetylcholine: postganglionic fibres release it onto muscarinic receptors of the gland.
cards.section: Lever 2: sweat, and its ceiling

cards.front: A person given a muscarinic receptor antagonist exercises in hot, dry air. Predict sweating, evaporative heat loss and core temperature. Would noradrenergic skin vasoconstriction in the cold be blocked?
cards.back: Sweating and evaporation fall, so more heat is stored. Cold vasoconstriction is not blocked: it uses noradrenaline, not acetylcholine on muscarinic receptors.
cards.why: Eccrine sweating is cholinergic muscarinic; cold vasoconstriction is noradrenergic.
cards.quote: postganglionic fibres release it onto muscarinic receptors of the gland
cards.section: Lever 2: sweat, and its ceiling

cards.front: Why does eccrine sweat leave the skin hypotonic, and why is it saltier at high flow?
cards.back: The secretory coil makes a near-plasma fluid; the duct reabsorbs sodium and chloride while staying relatively impermeable to water. At high flow the duct has less time per millilitre, so less salt is reclaimed.
cards.quote: Sweat leaves hypotonic, and saltier at high flow, when the duct has less time per millilitre.
cards.section: Lever 2: sweat, and its ceiling

cards.front: In the eccrine sweat duct, chloride is reabsorbed through {{c1::CFTR}}.
cards.quote: the duct reabsorbs sodium and chloride (chloride through CFTR, see membrane transport) while staying relatively impermeable to water.
cards.section: Lever 2: sweat, and its ceiling

cards.front: Suppose the CFTR channels of a person's sweat ducts conduct no chloride. Predict the chloride content of the sweat that reaches the skin, compared with normal.
cards.back: Sweat chloride would be higher than normal, since less is reclaimed by the duct, so the sweat is saltier and more salt is lost per litre.
cards.why: Rests on the rule that the duct reclaims chloride through CFTR, turning a near-plasma primary fluid into hypotonic sweat.
cards.quote: The secretory coil makes a primary fluid close to plasma in osmolality
cards.section: Lever 2: sweat, and its ceiling

cards.front: Why does heavy sweating raise plasma osmolality, and what responses follow?
cards.back: Sweat is hypotonic, so it removes more water than salt: plasma volume falls and osmolality rises, driving ADH release and thirst.
cards.quote: Heavy sweating therefore loses more water than salt: plasma volume falls and osmolality rises, driving ADH release and thirst
cards.section: Lever 2: sweat, and its ceiling

cards.front: Each gram of sweat that evaporates at skin temperature carries off about {{c1::2.43 kJ}} of heat, its latent heat of evaporation.
cards.back: 2.26 kJ per g is the value at 100 °C, not skin temperature. A gram that drips carries away almost none.
cards.quote: each gram that does carries off about 2.43 kJ of heat at skin temperature, its latent heat of evaporation
cards.section: Why humid air sets a ceiling

cards.front: Wet skin at 35 °C saturates the air touching it at about 5.6 kPa. Air at 35 °C holds about 2.2 kPa of water vapour at 40 percent humidity and 4.5 kPa at 80 percent. Find each vapour-pressure gap and how E_max compares, other things equal.
cards.back: 40%: 5.6 − 2.2 = 3.4 kPa. 80%: 5.6 − 4.5 = 1.1 kPa, about a third as large. E_max scales with the gap, so at 80 percent it is roughly a third, with the same air movement and clothing.
cards.quote: At 80 percent humidity the air holds about 4.5 kPa, and the gap shrinks to about 1.1 kPa, a third as large.
cards.section: Why humid air sets a ceiling

cards.front: A cyclist must lose 850 W by evaporation, but humid air allows at most 700 W. Her skin is already fully wet. Would doubling her sweat rate stop heat storage?
cards.back: No. Extra sweat drips instead of evaporating, so it adds dripping, not cooling. Evaporation cannot exceed 700 W, so at least 150 W is stored.
cards.quote: If her skin is already fully wet, the rest drips and sweating harder adds dripping, not cooling.
cards.section: Why humid air sets a ceiling

cards.front: Made-up example: a 60 kg runner needs 600 W of evaporation. Latent heat 2.43 kJ per g; 1 g sweat = 1 mL. What sweat rate is needed if every gram evaporates, and if only 75 percent does? Without drinking, what percent of body mass is lost per hour with the 75 percent case?
cards.back: 600 J/s ÷ 2,430 J/g × 3,600 s/h = 889 g/h, about 0.89 L/h. At 75 percent: 889 ÷ 0.75 = 1,185 g/h, about 1.19 L/h. Mass loss 1.185 ÷ 60 = about 2.0 percent per hour.
cards.quote: Sweat needed if every gram evaporates: 850 J per s ÷ 2,430 J per g = 0.350 g per s
cards.section: Why humid air sets a ceiling

cards.front: Made-up example: an 80 kg worker has heat production 820 W and dry heat gain 80 W; humid air caps evaporation at 750 W. Assuming uniform body temperature and specific heat 2.98 kJ per kg per °C, how fast does body temperature rise?
cards.back: S = 820 + 80 − 750 = 150 W = 540 kJ per hour. Heat capacity = 80 × 2.98 = 238.4 kJ per °C. Rise = 540 ÷ 238.4 = about 2.3 °C per hour.
cards.quote: Heat capacity: 70 kg × 2.98 kJ per kg per °C = 208.6 kJ per °C.
cards.section: Why humid air sets a ceiling

cards.front: With heat production, dry heat gain and E_max all held fixed, what are the only three ways to restore heat balance?
cards.back: Make less heat (slow down), gain less dry heat (shade, cooler air), or raise E_max (drier or faster-moving air, less clothing).
cards.quote: make less heat (slow down), gain less dry heat (shade, cooler air), or raise E_max (drier or faster-moving air, less clothing)
cards.section: Why humid air sets a ceiling

cards.front: In a real person with E_req above E_max, why does heating often slow toward a new steady state, and when is heat stress called uncompensable?
cards.back: Warmer skin raises the vapour pressure of its sweat, raising E_max, and shrinks dry heat gain, lowering E_req. Heat stress is uncompensable when no such steady state exists.
cards.quote: Heat stress becomes uncompensable when no such state exists, which is what the chamber studies below look for.
cards.section: Why humid air sets a ceiling

cards.front: During an hour of exercise in humid heat without drinking, why does stroke volume fall while heart rate rises?
cards.back: Sweat loss shrinks plasma volume, and the faster heart shortens filling time, so cardiac filling and stroke volume fall.
cards.why: How much pooling of blood in skin veins adds during exercise is debated.
cards.quote: Sweat loss shrinks plasma volume and the faster heart shortens filling time, so cardiac filling and stroke volume fall.
cards.section: When the ceiling is too low

cards.front: In 7 trained cyclists exercising in 35 °C heat, cutaneous vascular resistance rose despite a higher oesophageal temperature. What does this show?
cards.back: When dehydration adds to hyperthermia, the skin circulation joins systemic vasoconstriction, cutting heat delivery to the skin just when it is needed.
cards.quote: When dehydration adds to hyperthermia, the skin circulation joins the systemic vasoconstriction, cutting heat delivery to the skin just when it is needed.
cards.section: When the ceiling is too low

cards.front: What feature separates heat stroke from heat exhaustion?
cards.back: Central nervous system dysfunction (confusion, seizures or coma) defines heat stroke, often with injury to other organs. Heat exhaustion is heat strain without marked CNS dysfunction.
cards.quote: Heat stroke is severe heat illness defined by central nervous system dysfunction, such as confusion, seizures or coma, often with injury to other organs.
cards.section: When the ceiling is too low

cards.front: A runner collapses during a hot race, is confused, and is still sweating heavily. Does the sweating rule out heat stroke?
cards.back: No. The confusion is CNS dysfunction, which defines heat stroke. Sweating often persists early in exertional heat stroke, so sweating does not mean heat balance.
cards.quote: Sweating often persists early in exertional heat stroke, so sweating does not mean heat balance.
cards.section: When the ceiling is too low

cards.front: How does sweating change with heat acclimation?
cards.back: Sweating starts earlier and rises more steeply with core temperature, and aldosterone lowers the sodium in sweat.
cards.quote: With repeated heat exposure, sweating starts earlier and rises more steeply with core temperature, and aldosterone lowers the sodium in sweat.
cards.section: When the ceiling is too low

cards.front: Young healthy adults at low metabolic rate sat in a chamber whose heat stress rose in steps while core temperature was recorded. How was each person's critical wet-bulb found, and how did the humid-air mean compare with the long-cited 35 °C limit?
cards.back: It was the inflection where the core-temperature trace stopped staying nearly flat and bent upward. In humid air the mean was about 30.5 °C wet-bulb, below 35 °C, because a living person also makes heat that must leave.
cards.quote: That bend, the inflection, marks the critical wet-bulb for that person.
cards.section: How humid is too humid?

cards.front: In adults in the cold, what mainly raises heat production, and what happens to it if core temperature keeps falling?
cards.back: Shivering muscle. Shivering wanes below a core temperature of about 31 °C.
cards.quote: if core temperature keeps falling, shivering wanes below about 31 °C.
cards.section: In the cold: constrict, shiver, burn brown fat

cards.front: How does brown adipose tissue make heat without muscle contraction?
cards.back: UCP1 lets protons leak back across the inner mitochondrial membrane without making ATP, so the gradient's energy becomes heat.
cards.quote: the protein UCP1 lets protons leak back across the inner mitochondrial membrane without making ATP, so the gradient's energy becomes heat
cards.section: In the cold: constrict, shiver, burn brown fat

cards.front: A chemical makes the inner mitochondrial membrane leaky to protons in all tissues, as UCP1 does in brown fat. Predict heat production and ATP made per unit of fuel oxidized.
cards.back: Heat production rises, because protons return without driving ATP synthesis and the gradient's energy becomes heat.
cards.why: Extends the stated UCP1 rule to every tissue; no new mechanism is assumed.
cards.quote: Brown adipose tissue makes heat without contraction
cards.section: In the cold: constrict, shiver, burn brown fat

cards.front: After mild cold, PET-CT found active brown fat in 23 of 24 healthy men, yet clinical scans without controlled cold found it in only about 3 to 8 percent. What reconciles the two, and what do these scans actually measure?
cards.back: Detection needs activation: many healthy men have brown fat that shows only when cold activates it. The scans trace FDG, a glucose analogue, so they report glucose uptake, not heat.
cards.why: Brown fat burns mostly fatty acids, so FDG uptake does not show how much heat it adds.
cards.quote: A review of clinical scans taken without controlled cold found it in about 3 to 8 percent, more often in cold weather.
cards.section: In the cold: constrict, shiver, burn brown fat

cards.front: Name the epidermal strata from deep to superficial. Which one is found only in thick skin?
cards.back: Basale, spinosum, granulosum, lucidum, corneum. The lucidum is found only in the thick skin of palms and soles.
cards.quote: divide in the stratum basale and move outward through the spinosum, the granulosum, a clear lucidum found only in the thick skin of palms and soles, and the corneum.
cards.section: The skin that does all this

cards.front: Keratinocytes end as {{c1::corneocytes}}: flat cells with no nucleus, packed with keratin.
cards.quote: ending as corneocytes: flat cells with no nucleus, packed with keratin.
cards.section: The skin that does all this

cards.front: Why does skin colour differ between people?
cards.back: Differences in the amount and type of melanin and in the size, distribution and fate of melanosomes. Melanocyte number is similar between people.
cards.quote: Skin colour differs with the amount and type of melanin and the size, distribution and fate of melanosomes, not with melanocyte number
cards.section: The skin that does all this

cards.front: What are Langerhans cells, where in the epidermis are they most prominent, and what do they do?
cards.back: Antigen-presenting cells, most prominent in the stratum spinosum, that carry antigen to lymph nodes.
cards.quote: Langerhans cells, antigen-presenting cells most prominent in the spinosum, carry antigen to lymph nodes
cards.section: The skin that does all this

cards.front: Elias and Friend followed electron-dense, water-soluble tracers between cells in neonatal mouse epidermis. If tight junctions were the seal, where should the tracers stop? Where did they stop, and what did that show?
cards.back: Expected: at tight junctions between living cells. Observed: in the upper stratum granulosum, where lamellar bodies had emptied lipid between cells. The main barrier is that extruded lipid.
cards.quote: Instead they moved between cells up to the upper stratum granulosum and stopped where lamellar bodies, lipid-filled granules, had emptied their contents into the space between cells.
cards.section: The water barrier is lipid between dead cells

cards.front: Mice lacking claudin-1 died within a day of birth with excess water loss through the skin. What does this add to the lipid model of the skin's water barrier?
cards.back: Tight junctions in the granular layer also contribute to the barrier, alongside the intercellular lipid, and the knockout shows what an uncontrolled leak costs.
cards.quote: mice lacking claudin-1 died within a day of birth with excess water loss through the skin
cards.section: The water barrier is lipid between dead cells

cards.front: In human skin, what drives each of the two steps from 7-dehydrocholesterol to vitamin D3, and where does most synthesis happen?
cards.back: UVB (290 to 315 nm) photolyses 7-dehydrocholesterol to previtamin D3; a temperature-dependent isomerization, not light, converts it to D3. Mostly in the living basale and spinosum.
cards.quote: a temperature-dependent isomerization, not light, converts that to vitamin D3.
cards.section: Sunlight makes vitamin D in the living epidermis

cards.front: Excised human skin is exposed to cloudless January sunlight in Boston (42.2 °N). Would previtamin D3 form? Why?
cards.back: No. In Boston none formed from November through February. Low winter sun passes through more atmosphere, where ozone absorbs UVB.
cards.why: This is photochemistry in vitro, not blood levels in people.
cards.quote: Low winter sun sends its light through more atmosphere, where ozone absorbs UVB.
cards.section: Sunlight makes vitamin D in the living epidermis

cards.front: Two people live at 52 °N, one with heavily pigmented skin, one with lightly pigmented skin. Predict previtamin D3 production in excised skin from midday sun in December, and say how pigmentation would matter at a site and season where synthesis does occur.
cards.back: December: neither makes any, since in Edmonton (52 °N) none formed from October through March (in vitro, excised skin). Where synthesis does occur, the more pigmented skin makes less per exposure and needs a longer exposure.
cards.why: Combines the latitude-season result with the rule that melanin absorbs UVB.
cards.quote: Melanin also absorbs UVB, so more pigmented skin makes less previtamin D3 from the same exposure
cards.section: Sunlight makes vitamin D in the living epidermis

cards.front: Why has sunlight not been reported to cause vitamin D toxicity?
cards.back: Further UVB converts excess previtamin D3 to lumisterol and tachysterol, which do not act as vitamin D3.
cards.quote: further UVB converts excess previtamin D3 to lumisterol and tachysterol, which do not act as vitamin D3
cards.section: Sunlight makes vitamin D in the living epidermis

cards.front: Design a test, in volunteers in cold water, of the claim that most body heat is lost through the head. Give the null prediction and key design features. What did such a study find?
cards.back: Null: loss in proportion to surface area (head about 7 percent). 2 x 2 design: head in or out, body insulated or not; suppress shivering. Result (8 men, 17 °C water, body uninsulated): head submersion added about 10 percent to total heat loss, yet the core cooled about 42 percent faster.
cards.quote: Null prediction: each region loses heat roughly in proportion to its surface area.
cards.section: Design problem

cards.front: A hiker walks in still, dry desert air at 45 °C, warmer than her skin. Which route must remove all her heat, and how much must it remove?
cards.back: Evaporation is the only exit. Dry exchange is now a gain, so evaporation must remove heat production plus the dry gain for storage to be zero.
cards.why: Rests on the heat budget and on the rule that once air is as warm as the skin, evaporation is the only exit.
cards.quote: once the air is as warm as the skin, it is the only exit.

cards.front: A worker in a vapour-impermeable protective suit does steady hard work in mild air and is soon dripping sweat. Predict core temperature, and which remedy works: drinking more, sweating more, or slowing down.
cards.back: Core temperature rises if the suit drops E_max below the heat that must go, and extra sweat just drips. Slowing down works by making less heat; more fluid or more sweat cannot raise E_max.
cards.why: Rests on two rules: clothing lowers E_max, and balance returns only by less heat, less dry gain or higher E_max.
cards.quote: It scales with that gap and with how fast moving air carries the vapour away; clothing lowers it.
cards.section: Why humid air sets a ceiling

cards.front: A heat-acclimated and an unacclimated person do the same work in humid air whose E_max is well below the heat they must lose. Does acclimation stop core temperature rising? When would it help most?
cards.back: No. Acclimation brings earlier, steeper sweating, but E_max is set by the air, so extra sweat drips and heat is still stored.
cards.why: Combines acclimation (earlier, steeper sweating) with the rule that sweat rate does not set E_max.
cards.quote: Sweat rate sets how much water is offered. The gap sets how much can leave.
cards.section: Why humid air sets a ceiling
